title: Why this site — positioning memo
description: Concept memo for Renee Miller: how the new site positions The Miller Group, what changed from millergroup.com, and what to verify before launch.

hero.lede: One page on the argument behind the build: the positioning, what moved, what we deliberately left off, and what only you can confirm.

body:
The one-line position

The agency marketers call when they’re stuck.

The buying question has moved from “who can do our marketing?” to “who can solve this particular problem?” Constrained budgets don’t remove problems; they make hiring more careful — which favors whoever can say “before you spend more, we’ll find where the money actually matters.” You have done exactly that for 36 years. StreetPulse is the mechanism, the 250+ engagements are the evidence, and the challenger definition is the filter that lets the wrong client leave politely.

The old homepage sold an audience at the top (“We turn overlooked brands into industry titans”) and asked for a problem at the bottom (“Tell us the question keeping your team in the conference room”). The ending already believed this positioning; the beginning didn’t. The new site makes the ending the beginning.

Diagnosis is the wedge, not the business

A promise to “find what’s holding your brand back” sells small if it stops there — it puts you next to brand trackers and AI-interview startups, and gets you handed off before the creative work where the margin is. Every page therefore shows the ladder in one breath: Ask. Aim. Make. — find out, decide where the money matters, make the work. The hero lede says it (“we don’t stop at the diagnosis”), the case format enforces it (question → found → made → happened), and Gelson’s leads everywhere because it is the whole ladder in one story.

What moved, page by page

TodayNew siteWhy
8-step “you’re looking for an agency” hero, no proof above the foldJob-first hero, four “Maybe…” lines, proof by section 03Situation before category; numbers before adjectives
Six flat services, no relationship between themAsk. Aim. Make. — one loop, three colorsShows research, strategy and creative compound
StreetPulse = one nav item of sevenOwn page, own gradient, own CTA, nav slotIt is the only proprietary thing you sell
14 equal work tiles; 4 of 14 carry a number, 2 of those buried elsewhereProof-first order, industry filters, a full page per case with the number leading“Have they done this for someone like me?” answered in one scroll
Four competing CTAsOne door: “Bring us the challenge” on every page; StreetPulse books a callOne site, one action, measurable
Quotes with no titles; team with no biosQuotes with organizations; team framed as “the people in the pitch”Credibility is in the attribution

Deliberately not on the site

  • The 80% stat. ~80% of ad dollars now go to retail media, search and social — true, useful in your strategy, but on your site it advertises that you don’t play in 80% of the spend.
  • The 56% stat as a headline. Leading with the buyer’s constraint is pain-first (the v1 “You’ll be outspent” problem). It is the reason for the offer in a pitch, never the hero.
  • “Faster/cheaper than a focus group.” Against AI-interview tools you lose that fight; the site claims what only you have — real people, on camera, in the street.
  • “Builds the right team around every assignment.” Reads as freelancer network to a buyer already worried you’re small, and contradicts “one senior team.”
  • Media as a service. Consistent with the 80% point — the site never claims a media department.

Only you can confirm

  • 250+ engagements and $1B+ client revenue — both from your draft; marked * on the site until confirmed.
  • Pocky +20% appears on your CPG industry page but not the case page — which is right?
  • Pier 39 “10,000 visitors a year” is almost certainly 10 million.
  • Quote titles. Yvonne Manganaro, Jered Gold, Dalita Lovett, Julia Diamond, Christianne Van Grunsven, Martha Guzman — a title next to each name roughly doubles the weight of the quote.
  • Salvation Army and simplehuman — any number the client will release turns a word-stat into a headline.
  • Team bios — one line each: what they have run, for whom.

The 30-day test

Show the site to 5–10 ideal buyers. Don’t ask them to react to the positioning — reacting gets politeness. Ask them to recall the last agency they hired and what the trigger was. If “we were stuck / we couldn’t figure out why X wasn’t working” comes back unprompted, the thesis is real; show the hero afterward as a confirmation check. Pre-commit the result that would make you drop it. Run one channel for 30 days; success is consistent “I’d hire her to…” answers plus leads from the channel.

How this site is built to change

Every word on every page lives in a plain content file (one per page, one per case); the design lives in one stylesheet; one command rebuilds the site. Adding a case is copying a file. Changing a color, a heading size or the CTA copy is one edit that updates every page. The same content files become the fields of a WordPress theme if you keep WordPress as the admin — nothing here is written twice.
